hero.lead: A free map for your money. See which step comes next and why, in plain words. No sign-up. Nothing you type is saved.

roadmap.title: Your 8-step money path
roadmap.intro: Each step makes the next one safer. Switch between two example people to see how the path changes.

notReady.label: Not ready yet
notReady.summary: Example person: owes $2,400 on a credit card at 24.9% APR and has $300 saved.

ready.label: Ready
ready.summary: Example person: no high-interest debt, bills covered, and $1,000 saved for emergencies.

roadmap.detailHint: Pick any step to read what it means.

explain.notReady: The light is red because debt over 15% APR grows faster than investments usually do. Paying off a 24.9% card is like earning a sure 24.9%. Investing waits until the debt is gone. That's the smart order, not a failure.
explain.ready: The light is green. Bills are covered, there's no high-interest debt, and there's a $1,000 cushion. Now it makes sense to grow the cushion and start learning about investing.

milestones.title: Cover the basics
milestones.body: Rent, food, utilities and getting to work come first. A simple plan for where each dollar goes helps you see what's left.

milestones.title: Open a fee-free bank account
milestones.body: A free FDIC-insured bank or NCUA-insured credit union account keeps your money safe and stops check-cashing fees from eating your pay.

milestones.title: Save a $1,000 cushion
milestones.body: A small emergency fund means a flat tire or a doctor bill doesn't turn into new debt. Small, regular amounts get you there.

milestones.title: Get your job's 401(k) match
milestones.body: If your job adds money when you save for retirement, that's extra pay. Saving enough to get the full match is usually worth it.

milestones.title: Pay off high-interest debt
milestones.body: Debt over 15% APR, like most credit cards, grows fast. Paying it off is one of the surest ways to keep more of your money.

milestones.title: Grow your cushion to 3–6 months
milestones.body: A bigger cushion covers a job loss or slow months. Gig workers often aim for the higher end because pay goes up and down.

milestones.title: Invest for retirement
milestones.body: With a safe base in place, regular saving in an IRA or more in a 401(k) can grow for decades. This is money for later, not for bills.

milestones.title: Invest in a regular account
milestones.body: Once retirement saving is on track, a regular (taxable) investment account can help with other long-term goals.

readiness.title: Are you ready to invest? Three quick questions
readiness.intro: Answer yes or no. Your answers stay on this page and disappear when you leave.

questions.q: Do you have any debt over 15% APR?
questions.hint: This includes most credit cards, payday loans and title loans.

questions.q: Do you have at least $1,000 saved for emergencies?
questions.hint: Money you could use today without borrowing.

questions.q: Are your basic bills covered each month?
questions.hint: Rent, food, utilities and getting to work.

readiness.pending: Answer all three questions to see your light.

results.stopBills: Start with the basics. When your bills are covered each month, every other step gets easier. Free help: a nonprofit credit counselor or the CFPB guides on the Help page.
results.stopDebt: Pay down debt over 15% APR before investing. Every dollar you pay on a 24.9% card saves you about 25 cents a year. That beats what investing usually earns.
results.wait: You're close. Build a $1,000 cushion first so a surprise bill doesn't send you back into debt. Even $5 or $10 a week adds up.
results.go: Your base is safe. You're ready to learn how investing works. Start with the Learn page, then try a practice account before using real money.

andon.title: Life happened? Press pause.
andon.body: Lost hours, a medical bill, a family need. Pausing your plan is part of the plan. Stop adding money, keep your cushion, and pick up again when you can. No guilt.

toyota.title: Three simple ideas behind the path
toyota.intro: These come from a car factory famous for steady, careful work. They work for money, too.

cards.name: Kaizen

cards.name: Jidoka

cards.name: Andon
cards.body: Anyone can stop the line when something's wrong. You can pause your plan too, without shame.

meta.title: Small steps, big future
meta.description: Slide from $5 to $100 a week and see how small, regular saving could grow over 10 to 60 years.

grow.title: Small steps, big future
grow.lead: This is Kaizen: tiny, steady steps. Move the sliders to see how a small weekly amount could grow over time.
grow.chartDesc: Lines show the balance each year at 4%, 6% and 8% growth, compared with the money you put in.
grow.gensIntro: Say you stop adding money and leave it alone. Here's how it could keep growing for your kids and grandkids, about 25 years each.
grow.inflation: These numbers don't include inflation, which means prices rising over time. Real growth is often lower. Investments can also lose value.
grow.how: We add your weekly amount for a full year (× 52), then grow the total once a year at 4%, 6% or 8%. For your kids and grandkids, we let the final amount keep growing for 25 more years each, with no new money added.
why: It builds the habit. The amount can grow later when your income does.
Time does most of the work. Starting small today often beats starting big later.
Gig pay goes up and down? Save $5 in slow weeks and more in good ones.
grow.readyCheck: Before investing, make sure your base is safe.

about.title: About this site
about.lead: Where You Want to Be is a free education project. It helps people who've been left out of money advice see a safe, clear order of steps, without shame and without sales pitches.
about.mission: In 2025, the typical White family held about $332,000 in wealth. The typical Black family held about $37,000. Many people are kept out by fees, jargon and apps that assume you already have money. We start where you are.
privacy: We don't collect anything about you.
No accounts, no cookies, no tracking, no ads.
The calculators run on your device. Numbers you type are never saved or sent anywhere.
The site loads nothing from other companies.
disclosure: This is education, not financial advice.
We don't recommend or sell any product, fund, stock or company.
We don't earn money from links. Outside links go only to free public and nonprofit resources.
For advice about your own situation, talk to a licensed professional. You can check anyone's license on FINRA BrokerCheck.
about.brokerCheck: Check a professional on FINRA BrokerCheck
about.ideas: We borrow three ideas from careful factory work: small steps (Kaizen), safety gates (Jidoka) and a pause button (Andon).

meta.title: Investing in plain words
meta.description: Index funds, single stocks and bond funds, explained simply: how risky each one is and what it costs each year.

learn.title: Three ways to invest, in plain words
learn.lead: Most investing comes down to three building blocks. Here is what each one is, how bumpy it can be, and what it costs each year.

costPicker.label: Show the yearly cost if you put in
costPicker.note: Costs are typical examples. Real costs depend on the fund you pick.

index.title: Index funds
index.plain: One fund that holds small pieces of hundreds of companies at once.
index.costNote: About 0.05% a year, a common cost for a broad index fund.
points: If one company does badly, it's only a tiny part of the fund.
Prices still go up and down with the whole market.
Low yearly costs are a big reason many people start here.

stock.title: Single stocks
stock.plain: A small piece of one company. Your money rides on how that one company does.
stock.costNote: No yearly fund fee. The cost is risk: all your money is tied to one company.
points: One piece of bad news can drop the price a lot in a day.
There's no spreading out, unless you buy many different stocks.
Many people keep single stocks to a small share of their money, if any.

bond.title: Bond funds
bond.plain: A fund that lends money to governments or companies, who pay it back with interest.
bond.costNote: About 0.10% a year, a common cost for a broad bond fund.
points: Usually moves up and down less than stocks.
Usually grows more slowly than stocks over long periods.
Bond prices can dip when interest rates rise.

learn.askTitle: Questions to ask before you choose
learn.askIntro: There's no single right answer. These questions help you decide what fits you.
ask: Is my base safe first? No debt over 15% APR, bills covered, and a $1,000 cushion.
When will I need this money? Money for the next 5 years usually shouldn't be invested.
How would I feel if it dropped 30% for a while? Try it with pretend money first.
What does it cost each year? Small yearly costs add up over decades.
Am I spreading my money out, or betting on one thing?
learn.checkIntro: Before you trust anyone with your money, look them up. These checks are free.
learn.checkBroker: Look up a broker or adviser
learn.checkBrokerBody: See if a person or firm is registered and whether they have a record of problems.
learn.checkBasicsBody: Free, plain guides from the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC).
learn.checkPro: A licensed, fee-only adviser can help with your full picture. Ask how they are paid before you start.

meta.title: Practice a market drop
meta.description: Watch a pretend $1,000 drop 30%, then learn calm steps for when it happens for real. No real money.

practice.title: Practice a market drop, with pretend money
practice.lead: Markets go down sometimes. Seeing it happen with pretend money first makes a real drop less scary.
practice.chartLabel: Line chart of the practice portfolio's value over time.

status.ready: Your pretend portfolio is worth $1,000. Press the button to see a 30% drop.
status.dropped: Your pretend portfolio is now worth $700. That's a 30% drop. This is pretend money.
status.recovered: In this example, the portfolio climbed back to about $1,050 over time. Example, not a promise.

practice.stepperTitle: What to know when it drops

steps.title: This has happened before
steps.body: Drops like this have happened many times. Markets have recovered over time, though not always quickly. Some recoveries took years.

steps.title: Selling now locks in the drop
steps.body: While you hold, the drop is only on paper. If you sell now, the drop becomes real. Many people regret selling in a panic.

steps.title: Spreading out softens the bumps
steps.body: Owning many different things, like an index fund plus some bonds, means one bad day hurts less.

steps.title: Only invest money you won't need for 5+ years
steps.body: Rent, bills and your emergency cushion should never be invested. Then a drop can't force you to sell.

practice.doneNote: You've seen all four steps. You can watch an example recovery, or reset and try again.
what: Practice investing, or paper trading, means buying and selling with pretend money. Nothing real is bought or sold.
Many investing apps offer a free practice account. It's a safe way to learn how prices move and how you feel when they do.
Watch out: a practice account is still run by a company that may want you to open a real account. You never have to.
before: Your bills are covered each month.
You have no debt over 15% APR.
You have at least $1,000 saved for emergencies.
The money you invest won't be needed for 5 years or more.
You know what it costs each year.

meta.title: Your path: steps for your stage of life
meta.description: Money steps for people 50 and older, gig workers, first-generation earners, and anyone moving from cash to a bank account.

path.title: Your path
path.lead: Everyone starts from a different place. Pick the story closest to yours to see the steps that matter most.
path.stepsNote: Tick steps as you read. Nothing is saved.

catchUp.name: Sunita, 58
catchUp.role: Office manager at a community services agency
catchUp.story: Sunita worried that saving after 50 wouldn't matter. Then she learned the rules give people her age extra room to save. She started from Day 1: this year.
facts: Up to {k401} more a year in a 401(k), on top of the normal limit.
Up to {ira} more a year in an IRA, on top of the normal limit.
catchUp.superCatchUp: If you're 60 to 63, a newer rule may let you save even more in a 401(k). Ask a licensed pro or your plan.
steps: Find out if your job offers a 401(k) and a match.
Use the extra 50+ room in a 401(k) or IRA, even a little at first.
Pay down debt over 15% APR. Each payment is a sure win.
Keep an emergency cushion, so you never need to pull from retirement savings early.
Look at Social Security timing. Starting later usually means a bigger monthly check.
catchUp.proNote: Retirement accounts and taxes have many rules. A licensed pro or free tax help (IRS VITA) can check your plan.

gig.name: Tariq, 31
gig.story: Tariq's pay changes every week. Big plans never stuck. A small rule did: $5 in slow weeks, more in good weeks.
steps: Pick a tiny weekly amount you can do even in a slow week, like $5.
In good weeks, add more to your cushion first.
Set aside a share of every payment for taxes. Gig pay has no tax taken out.
Keep tax money in a separate account so it's not spent by mistake.
Aim for a bigger cushion than most, because your pay goes up and down.
gig.taxTip: Gig income is reported on a 1099 form. Free tax help is available.
gig.toolLabel: See what $5 a week can grow to

firstGen.name: Ayanna, 24
firstGen.role: First-generation college grad, clinical data coordinator
firstGen.story: Ayanna has a 24.9% credit card and a job that matches 401(k) savings. She wasn't sure which came first. Now she has a clear order.
steps: Save a $1,000 cushion so surprises don't go on the card.
Save enough in your 401(k) to get the full match. It's extra pay.
Then put every extra dollar toward debt over 15% APR.
Once that debt is gone, grow your cushion to 3–6 months.
Then start learning about investing more for retirement.
firstGen.rule: The simple rule: get the match, then pay off debt over 15% APR before investing more.

banked.name: Guadalupe, 38
banked.role: Home health aide and family caregiver
banked.story: Guadalupe paid a check casher every payday. That fee added up to hundreds of dollars a year. A free, insured account changed that.
steps: Find a bank or credit union with no monthly fee and no minimum balance.
Check that it's FDIC-insured (banks) or NCUA-insured (credit unions).
Bring a photo ID. Many places accept a passport, consular ID or ITIN.
Set up direct deposit so your pay goes straight in, for free.
Start your $1,000 cushion in the same account, a little each payday.
banked.fdic: If an insured bank or credit union closes, the government protects your money, up to $250,000 per person.

path.pauseTitle: Every path has a pause button
path.pause: Lost hours, a medical bill, a family need: life happens. Pausing your plan is part of the plan. Keep your cushion, stop adding for a while, and pick up again when you can.
